## TL;DR

Resumed task #1185 after handoff was rejected because its engineering report draft was missing. The implementation already covered Linux systemd cgroup detection, launchd detection, and hand-run classification, but review found no regression test for the Linux systemd-parent fallback. Added a test matching the reported renamed service process and recorded that real hand-run restart QA was not performed. The scoped RepoOS check is the remaining validation step for this resumed session.

## Work and rationale

I began by checking the assigned absolute worktree, branch, dirty state, active task listing, and handoff status. The branch was clean at the start of the resumed turn. The worktree task copy showed review, but the RepoOS board/list output reported #1185 as active with its engineer still running, so I continued on the assigned task branch and did not edit task metadata.

The unresolved review finding specifically called out coverage for `/proc/<pid>/cgroup` or systemd-parent fallback. Inspection showed two cgroup tests were already present: one for a renamed RepoOS managed user unit and one for an external unit after ignoring `user@<uid>.service`. There was also coverage for a shell-parented hand-run process and an uncertain systemd-parent case without a unit. What was missing was a positive systemd-parent test proving that a renamed RepoOS unit is recognized when both `systemctl status` and cgroup lookup fail.

I added a focused test to `src/core/supervisor-detect.test.ts`. It supplies a non-shell parent command of `/lib/systemd/systemd --user` containing `com.repoos.serve.tuk-driver-aaa442e5.service`; the expected result is `managed` with the unit name stripped of `.service`. This reproduces the relevant supervisor identity in the problem report and protects the fallback branch from regressing to hand-run detection.

I reviewed the existing QA record. It already stated that restart was not performed against a real hand-run server or a live systemd/launchd instance. I added a short note documenting that this resumed session did not operate a real server either, so automated regression coverage is not misrepresented as live operator QA. This fulfills the task's either/or QA note without claiming an unobserved outcome.

The earlier implementation and QA evidence remain as recorded: the notification supports systemd/launchd/hand-run/uncertain states, restart actions display pending feedback and errors, and UI/server tests cover restart behavior. I did not alter those flows during this repair because the review finding was a missing detector test, not a newly observed behavior defect.

## Approaches tried

I first inspected the detector and test file rather than duplicating existing cases. This revealed the positive cgroup fallback was already covered and narrowed the repair to the parent fallback. I then added an isolated test with mocked command execution, preserving deterministic coverage without depending on the host's actual init system or process tree.

I checked the current RepoOS handoff status and observed the exact prior failure: the engineering report draft was missing. This report draft addresses that prerequisite; RepoOS will bind/finalize it against the checked tree during handoff processing.

## Challenges and blockers

No live hand-run server or systemd/launchd instance was available for this resumed work, so I cannot claim a real restart was performed. The QA document explicitly records this limitation. The branch task copy and central board status had differed at inspection time; the live list showed the task active, and I left task status under RepoOS control.

The initial requested check has not yet been run at the time this draft was written. The work is not ready for handoff until `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passes.

## Key learnings

The Linux detector's positive systemd cgroup route had test coverage, but that did not exercise the separate parent-command fallback used after cgroup access fails. A dedicated test for each independent fallback is important because the reported failure occurs precisely when process naming no longer identifies RepoOS. Also, automated UI fixtures and detector tests do not substitute for a real restart; the QA note must keep that distinction explicit.
